source_text: Let's keep the list in the same mission document for concision, but yes, please draft it now.  And, yes, what I'm now thinking is that the "tool" layer is really just part of an SVO triple where the verbs are already part of our intent layer.  So, e.g., "ask, constrain responses" might be an example.  The point is to try to make the human side reasonably familiar without anthropomorphising the agent or tool.  Even in a case where we might "delegate" the act of paying to an agent or subagent, I think it would be a bit silly to talk about them "forming an opinion" or whatever.  I might use that kind of language informally to get my point across *to* an agent, but for the ontology, it's much more cut-and-dried.

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) The draft is in the mission as §3, "DERIVE (draft): operator intents as SVO", committed and pushed as `abf6171`. It has six rules and 20 triples built from GLOSS, plus a short list of verbs the 象 set is missing.

㊢ (the rules) The subject is always the operator. The verb has to be one of the 21 象 intents, and any verb that isn't goes on the gap list rather than being invented in the row. Each row then gives:
- the **object**
- the **actions** the tool performs, described mechanically
- the **vendor words**, kept only so you can look a name up
- the FUTON counterpart
- a **fidelity check**: how you'd know the action carried out the intent

Your example becomes row 3: *ask-action + constrain · responses to a fixed set of typed answers*, via "call a classifier that returns a label and a probability". The check is that the stated probabilities match what's observed.

㊢ ("delegate the act of paying") Row 18 is *delegate · payment*, via "spend from a funded wallet up to a limit". The check is that spending stays within the limit and each purchase traces back to a task. That leaves nothing for an opinion to attach to. Payment is the object, so **pay** doesn't need to be a verb. The only real gap so far is **compare** (Braintrust's A-vs-B), which *explore* doesn't capture.

🈖 (what the draft shows) Ten of the tools fall under *delegate* or *verify*, which is where most of the selling is. The three rows with no FUTON counterpart (3 typed answers, 8 access scope, 18 spending limit) are all *constrain*. Rule 1 also removes the vendor words without losing anything. "The agent decides / learns / steers" only ever filled the subject slot.

🈳 (open) Rows 14 and 19 are the shakiest. In row 14 I made the operator's intent *collect/explore* run events, because the stream is something the operator wants to watch, not something the agent "reports". In row 19, p2r has every participant report their own work, agents included. So it may be the one tool that breaks rule 1, or it may just be a schema.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) Agreed. I've recorded this in the mission as tension T8, in your words, splitting the vocabulary into three layers: the operator's **intent**, the tool's **action**, and the **vendor word** for that action. It's committed and pushed as `77946a2`. I also added a caveat to GLOSS, because its verbs ("remember", "learn", "decide") are mostly vendor words. It works for translating the names, but it isn't the ontology.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
("intents (per speech act) and, let's say, actions") Take "memory" as an example:
- **Intent:** the operator's. Roughly *constrain* or *collect*: "don't make me repeat myself", "keep what we settled".
- **Action:** write facts to a graph or vector store, retrieve by similarity, inject the matches into the session.
- **Vendor word:** "memory".

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (what this does to the ontology idea) The rows of the "what people do when they do tech" list would be **operator intents**, which the 象 marks already cover as speech acts. Each row would say which actions carry that intent in which tools, including FUTON. The vendor words would be a lookup column, and the last column would ask how anyone could tell whether the intent was carried. Under that layout, tools that sound different ("memory", "context engine", "second brain") would land on the same actions. Tools with similar names could also turn out to carry different intents. Your earlier point about T7 now fits as a special case: speech acts belong to layer 1, and tool verbs like *lease* or *admit* belong to layer 2.

previous_reply_acts.text: (one decision) Shall I draft `landscape/ACTIVITIES.md` in that shape: intent → actions → vendor words → fidelity check? I'd fill a few rows from GLOSS to see whether the layout holds up before doing all of them.
